classification.difficultyReason: The earlier parts scaffold the algebra and perpendicular bisector; the main connection is using that bisector to justify a kite and its perpendicular-diagonal area.

content.prompt:
The line $2y-x=12$ intersects the circle $x^2+y^2-10x-12y+36=0$ at the points $A$ and $B$.
A sketch is given; it would be useful to add to it as you go through parts a to d.

spec.description: Unticked, ungridded axes arrowed at both ends, with an unlabelled red circle and blue rising line. No origin, centre or intersection labels are supplied.
spec.mathematics: Circle (x-5)^2+(y-6)^2=25 and line y=x/2+6; intersections (0,6) and (8,10).
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied curves and axes are visible; numerical coordinates and construction marks are absent.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{x}{2}+6\\x^2+\left(\frac{x}{2}+6\right)^2-10x-12\left(\frac{x}{2}+6\right)+36&=0\\\frac54x^2-10x&=0\\x(x-8)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }8\end{align*}$$
Substitute into $y=\frac{x}{2}+6$:
$$\begin{align*}x=0:\quad y&=6\\x=8:\quad y&=10\end{align*}$$
The coordinates are $(0,6)$ and $(8,10)$.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is the perpendicular line passing through the midpoint of $AB$.

answer.worked:
Midpoint of $AB$:
$$M=\left(\frac{0+8}{2},\frac{6+10}{2}\right)=(4,8).$$
Gradient of $AB$:
$$m_{AB}=\frac{10-6}{8-0}=\frac12.$$
The perpendicular bisector has gradient $-2$ and passes through $(4,8)$.
$$\begin{align*}y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\y-8&=-2(x-4)\\y&=-2x+16\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt:
The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ intersects the circle at the points $P$ and $Q$.
Find the exact coordinates of $P$ and $Q$.

answer.worked:
Substitute $y=-2x+16$ into the circle equation:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+(-2x+16)^2-10x-12(-2x+16)+36&=0\\5x^2-50x+100&=0\\x^2-10x+20&=0\\(x-5)^2&=5\\x&=5\pm\sqrt5\end{align*}$$
Substitute into $y=-2x+16$:
$$\begin{align*}x=5+\sqrt5:\quad y&=-2(5+\sqrt5)+16\\y&=6-2\sqrt5\\x=5-\sqrt5:\quad y&=-2(5-\sqrt5)+16\\y&=6+2\sqrt5\end{align*}$$
Thus $P$ and $Q$ have coordinates $(5+\sqrt5,6-2\sqrt5)$ and $(5-\sqrt5,6+2\sqrt5)$, in either order.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Explain why $APBQ$ is a kite and hence find its area.

answer.short: Since $P$ and $Q$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, $PA=PB$ and $QA=QB$, so $APBQ$ is a kite. Its area is $20\sqrt5$ square units.
answer.worked:
Since $P$ and $Q$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, $PA=PB$ and $QA=QB$. These are two pairs of equal adjacent sides, so $APBQ$ is a kite. Its diagonals $AB$ and $PQ$ meet at right angles.
Using the distance formula:
$$\begin{align*}AB&=\sqrt{(8-0)^2+(10-6)^2}\\AB&=\sqrt{80}\\AB&=4\sqrt5\\PQ&=\sqrt{(2\sqrt5)^2+(-4\sqrt5)^2}\\PQ&=\sqrt{100}\\PQ&=10\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12\times AB\times PQ\\\text{Area}&=\frac12\times4\sqrt5\times10\\\text{Area}&=20\sqrt5\text{ square units}\end{align*}$$
